triples.rationale: Ecclesiastes describes making gardens and planting every kind of fruit tree. Genesis describes God planting Eden's garden and causing trees good for food to spring up. The concrete shared pattern is a planted garden with edible trees; the royal experiment is not identified with Eden or assigned its tree of life.
triples.source_text: I made gardens and parks for myself and planted in them every kind of fruit tree.

target_units.text: And the Lord God planted a garden in Eden, toward the east, and there He placed the man whom He had formed.
And God caused every tree that was beautiful to behold and good for food to spring up from the earth, with the tree of life in the midst of the garden, and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.

triples.relationship: Irrigation used literally and as a teaching image
triples.rationale: Ecclesiastes constructs water pools to irrigate growing woodland. Sirach compares the speaker to a river channel entering a garden and speaks of watering a garden bed, before applying the flowing image to instruction. Both picture directed water nourishing cultivated growth; Sirach's figurative channel is not claimed to be the same physical pool or woodland.
triples.source_text: I made pools of water for myself to irrigate from them a woodland sprouting trees.

target_units.text: I too came out like a channel from a river, like a watercourse into a garden.
I said, “I will water my garden and drench my garden bed.” Then behold, my channel became a river, and my river became a sea.

triples.rationale: Ecclesiastes includes a time to keep and a time to throw away. The storm narrative gives a concrete occasion for discarding previously useful cargo and ship's tackle. This illustrates the disposal half of the saying under danger, without making the whole time catalogue a prediction of that voyage.
triples.source_text: a time to seek and a time to lose, a time to keep and a time to throw away,

target_units.text: As we were violently battered by the storm, the next day they began throwing cargo overboard.
On the third day they threw the ship’s tackle overboard with their own hands.

triples.relationship: Contrasting periods of war and peace
triples.rationale: Ecclesiastes places a time of war beside a time of peace. David recounts his great wars and God's promise of rest, peace and quietness in Solomon's days. Chronicles supplies a particular contrast between such periods, while the separate love-and-hate pair is not assigned to either king.
triples.source_text: a time to love and a time to hate, a time of war and a time of peace.

target_units.text: But the Lord’s word came upon me, saying, ‘You have poured out much blood and waged great wars. You shall not build a house for My name, because you have poured out much blood upon the earth before Me.

Behold, a son is born unto you; he shall be a man of rest. I will give him rest from all the enemies round about him, for Solomon is his name; and I will give peace and quietness unto Israel in his days.

triples.rationale: Ecclesiastes names warmth as a benefit when two lie down together. When clothing does not warm David, his attendants seek a woman to lie with him, and Abishag keeps him warm. The narrative concretely shares the bodily-warmth benefit; its explicit statement that David did not know her is preserved rather than making the comparison sexual.
triples.source_text: Also, if two lie down, they have warmth; but how can one be warm alone?

target_units.text: King David was old and advanced in days; and they wrapped him in garments, but he did not grow warm.
His attendants said, “Let them seek a young virgin for our lord the king. She shall attend the king and keep him warm; she shall lie with him, and our lord the king will become warm.”
And they sought a fair young woman throughout all the territory of Israel, and found Abishag the Shunammite, and brought her to the king.
The young woman was very fair; she kept the king warm and served him, but the king did not know her.

triples.relationship: Stillbirth described through absence of light
triples.rationale: In context Ecclesiastes speaks of a stillborn child whose departure and covered name are in darkness. Job compares his wished-for rest with a miscarriage or infants who never saw light. Both use the stillborn child's separation from the light of life in reflections on suffering; Job does not supply the separate detail of a name covered in darkness.
triples.source_text: for it came in futility and goes in darkness, and in darkness its name will be covered,

target_units.text: or like a miscarriage coming out of a mother’s womb, or like infants who never saw light.

triples.rationale: Ecclesiastes says it is unwise to ask why former days were better. Numbers recounts Israel's claim that it was well with them in Egypt and rebukes their disobedient lament over leaving. The narrative is a particular instance of a criticized favorable comparison with the past, without claiming every recollection of earlier days is wrong.
triples.source_text: Do not say, “What happened that the former days were better than these?” For it was not in wisdom that you asked about this.

target_units.text: And you shall say unto the people: Purify yourselves for tomorrow, and you shall eat meat; for you wept before the Lord, saying: Who will feed us meat? For it is well with us in Egypt. And the Lord will give you meat to eat, and you shall eat meat.
You shall eat not for one day, nor for two, nor for five days, nor for ten days, nor for twenty days;

for a whole month you shall eat, until it comes out of your nostrils, and it shall be unto you a bilious sickness; because you disobeyed the Lord, who is among you, and wept before Him, saying: Why did we come out of Egypt?

triples.relationship: Oil on the head alongside enjoyed provision
triples.rationale: Ecclesiastes urges an oiled head in a setting of glad eating and drinking. The psalm joins a prepared table, a head enriched with oil and an excellent cup. Both associate head-anointing with enjoyed provision; the psalm does not mention the white garments or identify a shared ritual.
triples.source_text: Let your garments be white at all times, and let oil not be lacking on your head.

target_units.text: Thou didst prepare a table before me opposite those who afflict me; Thou didst enrich my head with oil, and Thy cup is intoxicating—how excellent!

triples.rationale: Ecclesiastes warns that splitting wood brings danger. Deuteronomy gives the concrete case of an axe's iron slipping while wood is cut, killing a neighbor and exposing the cutter to an avenger. Both recognize woodcutting's dangers, while the legal example distinguishes the neighbor's immediate injury from the cutter's ensuing danger.
triples.source_text: Whoever lifts stones will be worn out by them; whoever splits wood will be endangered by it.

target_units.text: And this shall be the ordinance for the slayer who shall flee thither and live: whosoever strikes his neighbour unintentionally, having borne him no hatred aforetime,

as when a man goes with his neighbour into the forest to gather wood, and his hand is jolted with the axe as he cuts the wood, and the iron slips from the wood and strikes his neighbour, so that he dies, he shall flee unto one of these cities and live;

lest the kinsman who avenges blood pursue the slayer while his heart is hot, and overtake him, if the way is long, and strike him mortally, so that he dies, though no sentence of death is due unto him, for he bore his neighbour no hatred aforetime.

triples.relationship: Serpent danger and the limits of charming
triples.rationale: Ecclesiastes says a bite without a whispered charm leaves no advantage for the charmer. The psalm pictures a deaf asp refusing to hear enchanters or a wise person's spell. Both connect dangerous serpents with ineffective charming; the proverb's absent charm and the psalm's refused charm are distinct circumstances.
triples.source_text: If the snake bites without a whispered charm, there is no advantage for the charmer.

target_units.text: Their fury is in the likeness of a serpent, like that of a deaf asp that stops up its ears,
which will not hear the voice of enchanters, or a spell being cast by a wise person.

triples.rationale: Ecclesiastes says wine gladdens the living while speaking of bread and money. The psalm similarly says wine gladdens the human heart, beside oil brightening the face and bread making the heart firm. This is a particular shared description of wine's gladness, without using the psalm to explain everything listening to money.
triples.source_text: They make bread for laughter, and wine gladdens the living, and everything will listen to money.

target_units.text: and wine gladdens the human heart, to brighten the face with oil, and bread makes the human heart firm.

deferred_source_units.source_text: If the clouds are full of rain, they pour it upon the earth; and if a tree falls to the south or to the north, in the place where the tree falls, there it will be.
deferred_source_units.reason: The actual Job 36:27-29 numbers raindrops, pours rain into a cloud and describes shaded clouds; it does not say full clouds pour rain upon earth. Its unusual old-things wording is preserved. The proposed cloud-rain comparison is not retained as the particular causal image of Ecclesiastes, and the fallen-tree statement has no new supported match.

unresolved_candidates.source_text: If the clouds are full of rain, they pour it upon the earth; and if a tree falls to the south or to the north, in the place where the tree falls, there it will be.

target_units.text: Drops of rain are numbered by Him, and they will be poured as rain into a cloud;
old things will flow, and He shaded clouds over countless mortals.
He appointed a time for cattle, and they know the order of their resting place.
At all these things, is your mind not astonished, and is your heart not changed away from the body?
